To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) tones are reduced in natural disyllables and (2) tones of reduced disylables are not identified as tones, but are recognized as words instead

(1) the onset of the first syllable is most likely to be removed, (2) the onset of second syllable is most susceptible to be deleted, and (3), when there is insufficient segmental information, lexical status seems to override any acoustic cues, and tones tend to be recognized as the tone of a real word throughout a continuum.

the onset of a syllable is most likely to be removed when disyllables are reduced; the lexical status of a disyllable affects the tone identification of its fully pronounced version; the lexical effect disappears when the onset is removed; and the lexical effect is still present in a partly reduced disylable, but is not as strong as in its fully pronounced version.
